title: Mimosa Hangover: Why Brunch Drinks Hit Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why mimosas and bottomless brunch leave you so hungover, how much alcohol is really in a mimosa, and practical ways to prevent and recover from a brunch hangover.
metaDescription: Why mimosas and bottomless brunch hit so hard: hidden alcohol, bubbles, empty stomachs and refills. How to prevent and recover from a mimosa hangover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a mimosa hangover is rarely about the mimosa itself. Sparkling wine and orange juice are no more toxic than any other drink with the same amount of alcohol. The problem is the setting. Mimosas taste like breakfast juice, get topped up before the glass is empty, and are usually drunk late in the morning on a light stomach, sometimes in the sun, sometimes with a 90-minute bottomless deal pushing you to keep up. By mid-afternoon, a lot of people have had the equivalent of a bottle of wine without ever feeling like they were drinking hard.

**The quick rules:** eat a proper meal before or at the start of brunch, ask for a glass of water with every mimosa, count your glasses (or at least the refills), and set a stopping point before you sit down. If you're doing bottomless, decide your number in advance rather than trying to get your money's worth. If you're already hungover, rehydrate, eat, rest, and skip the "one more mimosa" fix.

> **When to get help.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within a day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if someone** can't be woken up, is confused, has slow or irregular breathing, keeps vomiting and can't keep water down, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, and they can happen at brunch just as easily as at a bar. Also see a doctor if you get severe stomach pain, vomit blood, faint, or feel your heart racing or skipping for more than a short while. If you notice shakes, sweating, or anxiety that only settle when you drink again, that's worth raising with a doctor too. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to watch for.

## Why Mimosas Hit Harder Than You Expect

A mimosa is simple: sparkling wine (often cheap prosecco, cava, or "champagne" in the loose sense) mixed with orange juice. Nothing in that recipe is unusually harsh. What makes the hangover feel out of proportion is a stack of small factors that all push in the same direction.

### 1. They don't taste like alcohol

Orange juice is sweet and tart, and it covers the taste of wine well. When a drink tastes like juice, you sip it like juice. People who would never finish four glasses of wine in an hour can finish four mimosas without thinking about it, because nothing tells them to slow down.

### 2. The bubbles may speed up absorption

Carbonated alcoholic drinks appear to get alcohol into your blood a bit faster than flat ones. A small study from the University of Surrey, published in 2007, found that most volunteers reached a higher blood alcohol level sooner after drinking sparkling champagne than after the same champagne gone flat. The usual explanation is that carbonation speeds up how quickly the stomach empties into the small intestine, where most alcohol is absorbed. The studies are small and the effect varies from person to person, but it fits what many people notice: bubbly drinks go to your head faster. Our article on [whether carbonation makes you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-carbonation-make-you-drunk-faster) goes into more detail.

Faster absorption doesn't change how much alcohol your body has to process. It does mean a higher peak, which makes it easier to lose track and keep drinking once your judgment slips.

### 3. Brunch often means a light or empty stomach

Food in your stomach is one of the most reliable ways to slow alcohol absorption. Many people arrive at brunch having skipped breakfast (it's brunch, after all), order a drink first, and wait 30 minutes or more for food. The first two or three mimosas land on an empty stomach, right when absorption is fastest.

### 4. The glass never empties

Refills are the core problem. When a server tops up your glass halfway through, you lose the natural count of "that's my third." A flute that looks like one drink might actually hold your third or fourth top-up. At bottomless brunches, staff are often encouraged to keep glasses full, and the mimosas can be poured heavier on the wine than you'd make at home.

### 5. Daytime drinking stacks with sun, heat, and a nap

Drinking outside on a patio in the sun adds fluid loss from sweating to the fluid loss alcohol already causes by making you pee more. Then there's the afternoon crash. Many people go home after brunch, nap for a couple of hours, and wake up at 5 p.m. feeling awful, because the hangover started while they slept. Alcohol also disrupts sleep quality, so the nap and the night that follows are often poor. For more on how daytime sessions play out, see our guide to [day drinking](/never-hungover/day-drinking).

## How Much Alcohol Is Actually in a Mimosa?

In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is roughly 5 ounces of wine at 12% alcohol. Most sparkling wine is around 11% to 12%. So the amount of alcohol in a mimosa depends almost entirely on how much wine goes into the glass.

| Mimosa style | Approximate sparkling wine | Rough standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Light home pour (1 part wine to 2 parts juice, 6 oz flute) | 2 oz | About 0.4 |
| Classic even pour (half and half, 6 oz flute) | 3 oz | About 0.6 |
| Bar-style pour (mostly wine, splash of juice) | 4 to 5 oz | About 0.8 to 1 |
| Large brunch glass or carafe-style serving (10 oz+, mostly wine) | 6 to 8 oz | About 1.2 to 1.6 |

These are rough figures to help you think, not exact measurements. The takeaway: a standard 750 ml bottle of sparkling wine holds about five standard drinks. If you've had eight bar-style mimosas, you've likely had well over a bottle of wine's worth of alcohol. Our page on [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine) has the full breakdown.

Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, give or take. That rate doesn't speed up because the drink is fizzy or because it's daytime. If you have ten mimosas between 11 a.m. and 1:30 p.m., your body is still working through that alcohol into the evening.

## The Bottomless Brunch Hangover

Bottomless brunch deals usually offer unlimited mimosas (or similar drinks) for a set price within a time limit, often 90 minutes to two hours. They're fun, social, and good value if you drink a lot. They're also close to a perfect setup for a bad hangover.

Here's why the format matters:

- **The clock encourages speed.** A time limit nudges people to drink fast to "get their money's worth," which pushes blood alcohol up quickly.
- **Counting becomes almost impossible.** With constant refills, most people have no idea how many drinks they've had.
- **Food often comes late.** Busy brunch kitchens can be slow, so early drinks go down before food arrives.
- **Group pace beats personal pace.** In a group, people tend to match the fastest drinker at the table.
- **It ends early, but the day doesn't.** Brunch ends in the early afternoon. Many groups move on to a bar, or people head home for a nap and a hangover that peaks by dinner.

### How to do bottomless brunch without wrecking your day

1. **Eat before you go, or order food the moment you sit down.** Ideally something with protein, fat, and starch, such as eggs, toast, and potatoes.
2. **Set your number in advance.** Decide that you'll have, say, three or four mimosas and stop there, regardless of the deal. Paying for unlimited drinks doesn't mean you have to drink them.
3. **Ask for water on the table and drink a glass between each mimosa.** It slows you down and offsets some fluid loss.
4. **Let your glass go empty before it's refilled.** If you can, turn down top-ups until you've finished. That keeps your count honest.
5. **Ask for more juice, less wine.** Most places will happily make yours lighter. You still get a mimosa; you just get less alcohol in each one.
6. **Sit in the shade if it's hot.** Heat plus alcohol plus sun dries you out quickly.
7. **Have a plan for after.** If the group is heading to a bar, consider switching to non-alcoholic drinks or leaving after brunch.

## Is It the Champagne, the Orange Juice, or the Sugar?

People often blame one ingredient for the mimosa hangover. Here's an honest look at each.

### The sparkling wine

The alcohol in the wine is the main cause of the hangover. Beyond that, wine contains small amounts of other compounds from fermentation, sometimes called congeners, and some research links drinks with more congeners (such as bourbon and red wine) to worse hangovers than clearer drinks. Sparkling white wine is generally on the lighter end. There is no good evidence that cheap sparkling wine causes worse hangovers than expensive bottles, though plenty of people swear that it does. For a deeper look at the drink itself, see our guides to the [champagne hangover](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and the [prosecco hangover](/never-hungover/prosecco-hangover).

**Sulfites** get a lot of blame for wine headaches. For most people, the evidence that sulfites cause hangover headaches is weak. They can trigger reactions in a small group of sensitive people, mostly those with asthma. Dried fruit typically contains more sulfites than wine does, so if apricots don't bother you, sulfites probably aren't your issue.

### The orange juice

Orange juice doesn't cause hangovers, and it doesn't prevent them either. It does two things worth knowing about:

- **It makes the drink easier to drink fast**, which is the indirect way it contributes.
- **It's acidic.** Orange juice plus alcohol plus an empty stomach can be a recipe for heartburn, reflux, or an upset stomach. If you tend to get acid reflux, that may be part of why mimosas leave you feeling worse than wine alone.

On the morning after, a glass of orange juice can be a reasonable source of fluid, sugar, and potassium, as long as your stomach can handle the acidity. Our guide to [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) covers that in more detail.

### The sugar

There is no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers. Sweet drinks mainly matter because they hide the taste of alcohol and go down quickly. Some people do feel shaky or weak after a sugary drinking session, which can be related to alcohol interfering with the liver's ability to keep blood sugar steady, especially when you haven't eaten much. That's one more reason to eat properly at brunch. Our guide to [the best and worst mixers](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) compares common options.

## What a Mimosa Hangover Feels Like

The symptoms are the same as any hangover. You may notice:

- Headache, often throbbing
- Tiredness and a heavy, foggy feeling
- Thirst and a dry mouth
- Nausea or an upset, acidic stomach
- Sensitivity to light and noise
- Feeling anxious, low, or on edge (often called "hangxiety")
- Poor sleep that night, even if you napped

What's different is the timing. Because brunch drinking ends in the early afternoon, the hangover often shows up the same day. You might feel great at 1 p.m., sleepy and flat by 3 p.m., and properly hungover by early evening. That's normal: hangover symptoms tend to peak as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero.

## How to Recover From a Mimosa Hangover

Nothing clears a hangover instantly. Your body has to finish processing the alcohol, and that takes time. These steps help you feel better while it does.

### Rehydrate steadily

Drink water in regular sips rather than chugging a liter at once, which can upset a queasy stomach. If you sweated in the sun or have been sick, an electrolyte drink can help replace salt and potassium. Our [electrolyte drinks comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) looks at the common options.

### Eat something gentle but real

Toast, rice, bananas, eggs, soup, or crackers are easy on the stomach and help bring your blood sugar back up. If the orange juice left you with heartburn, steer clear of more citrus, coffee, and spicy food until your stomach settles.

### Use pain relief carefully

A standard dose of ibuprofen or another NSAID, taken with food, can help a headache if it's safe for you. NSAIDs can irritate a stomach that's already upset by alcohol and acid, so don't take them on an empty stomach, and skip them if you have ulcers, kidney problems, or take blood thinners. Avoid stacking acetaminophen (Tylenol) on top of a heavy drinking day. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why. If you're unsure, ask a pharmacist.

### Rest, but protect tonight's sleep

A short nap is fine, but a three-hour nap at 4 p.m. can wreck your night's sleep and drag the hangover into tomorrow. If you can, keep naps short and aim for a normal bedtime.

### Skip the "hair of the dog" mimosa

Having another mimosa can numb the symptoms for a while, but you're just adding more alcohol for your body to process and pushing the hangover later. If you find you regularly need a drink to feel normal the morning after, that's worth talking to a doctor about.

## How to Prevent a Mimosa Hangover Next Time

The most effective step is simply drinking less alcohol in total. Beyond that, a few habits make a big difference:

- **Eat first.** A real meal before or at the start of brunch is the single best way to slow absorption.
- **Make it lighter.** Ask for more juice and less wine, or alternate mimosas with plain orange juice or sparkling water with a splash of juice.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour. With bar-style mimosas, that's close to one glass per hour.
- **Match each drink with water.** One glass of water per mimosa is an easy rule to follow.
- **Count your glasses.** Let the glass empty before accepting a refill so you know where you stand.
- **Stay cool.** Pick shade on hot days and keep drinking water.
- **Plan your afternoon.** Decide in advance whether you'll stop after brunch.

For the habits with the best evidence across all kinds of drinking, see our main guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### What about supplements?

Some people take a supplement before or during a brunch session. Here's an honest view. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement lets you drink a bottomless brunch's worth of mimosas without consequences, and it's no substitute for food, water, and pacing. If you'd like to try it alongside those habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- A mimosa hangover is mostly about how much you drank, not the drink itself. Juice hides the alcohol, refills hide the count, and bubbles may speed it into your blood.
- A bar-style mimosa can be close to one standard drink, and a bottomless brunch can add up to more than a bottle of wine.
- Eat a real meal early, drink water between glasses, ask for lighter pours, and set your limit before you sit down.
- To recover, rehydrate, eat gentle food, use pain relief carefully, and keep tonight's sleep on track.
- Confusion, trouble breathing, nonstop vomiting, or someone who can't be woken are signs of alcohol poisoning. Call 911.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do mimosas give me such a bad hangover?**

Usually it's the amount, not the drink. Mimosas taste like juice, come in small glasses that get topped up, and are often drunk on an empty or light stomach in the late morning. The bubbles in sparkling wine may also speed up how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Add sun, little water, and a long session, and you can end up drinking a full bottle of wine or more without noticing.

**How many mimosas does it take to get drunk?**

It depends on your size, how much you've eaten, and how the drink is poured. A typical mimosa with about 3 ounces of sparkling wine is a little over half a standard drink, but bar pours are often heavier on the wine. Three or four mimosas in an hour on an empty stomach is enough to make many people noticeably tipsy, and a bottomless brunch can easily reach eight or more.

**Is a bottomless brunch hangover worse than a normal hangover?**

It often feels worse because of how bottomless brunches work: a fixed time window that encourages fast drinking, refills that make it hard to count, drinking on a light stomach, and often sun and heat. Many people then nap in the afternoon, wake up feeling rough by early evening, and sleep badly that night. The symptoms are the same as any hangover, but the pattern makes heavy drinking easy.

**Does the orange juice in a mimosa help prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that the orange juice in a mimosa protects you from a hangover. It adds a little fluid, sugar, and vitamin C, but not nearly enough to offset the alcohol, and its sweetness can make the drink go down faster. The juice is also acidic, which can bother your stomach alongside alcohol. Drinking plain water between mimosas does far more.

**Can you get a hangover from just two or three mimosas?**

Some people can. Light drinkers, people who drink on an empty stomach, and people who are sensitive to wine can feel off after only a few. For most people, though, two or three properly poured mimosas spread over a meal won't cause much of a hangover. Trouble usually starts when the glass keeps getting refilled and you lose count.

**What should I eat before a bottomless brunch?**

Eat a real meal with protein, some fat, and some starch, or order food as soon as you sit down and eat it before your second drink. Eggs, toast, potatoes, and similar brunch staples all work. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, which lowers your peak blood alcohol and makes it easier to pace yourself.

**How do I get rid of a mimosa hangover fast?**

Nothing clears a hangover instantly, because your body has to finish processing the alcohol. What helps most is water or an electrolyte drink, a meal with some salt and carbohydrate, rest, and time. A standard dose of ibuprofen with food can ease a headache if it's safe for you. Avoid more alcohol, since a 'hair of the dog' mimosa only delays the hangover.
